subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, February 17, the debate on the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his opening remarks on Thursday last the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) made a very brief reference to the post-war depression which had been so evident in Canada in 1920 and 1921, and the gradual improvement in each budget brought down since he had been acting as Minister of Finance. He was becomingly modest in that he did not as usual give to his budgets the credit for all the improvements that had taken place. It is fortunate for the minister that he has held the portfolio of finance during the years in which the country

The Budget-Mr. Coote
has been recovering from the effects of its postwar deflation, and in which an improvement has been taking place.
I feel that if we were to analyse the matter we would find that credit for the improvement must be given largely to the primary producers of this country. Canada is primarily an agricultural country; agriculture is her basic industry, and the agricultural class were the worst sufferers from the deflation in 1920 and 1921. The purchasing power of the farmers' dollar, in many cases, dropped below fifty cents as compared with pre-war times, yet our farmers never stopped producing. The acreage which they sowed to wheat would be an indication of the way in which they tackled their . problem. Let me quote the acreage for a few years during this period:
Year	Acres
1921		23,000,000
1922		 22,400,000
1923		 22,671,000
It is true that a large number of farmers were forced off the land, but the acreage sown to wheat shows the spirit in which they tackled their problem. They did not rush to the government for relief or for a higher tariff. They tackled their problem in their own way.
I might remark in passing that the improved condition in which the Canadian National Railways stand to-day is largely attributable to the same cause. The credit for that should be given to the producers of this country who went ahead and produced, not knowing whether there would be a market for their product or at what price it might be sold. They were willing to take a chance on the world price. I am reminded of a statement made by Sir Thomas White when, as Minister of Finance he was floating one of our victory loans. He said that if this debt were ever to be repaid it would be from the top six inches of Canadian soil. The improved condition of our farmers, due largely to their own efforts, is responsible, to a considerable extent for the easy financing which the Minister of Finance referred to in his opening remarks. When the farmers are prosperous, business is good and government financing is made easy.
Many compliments have been handed to the Minister of Finance because of his brief and plain statement in the budget speech. It certainly is a very brief statement; it has every appearance of having been prepared in a hurry and with the idea of getting it through the House of Commons in a hurry. The minister neglected to tell us what the net debt of Canada is. There is no statement whatever in regard to our railway financing, and it seems to me that the budget is not complete without some reference to it. The minister should also have included in his statement details of the revenues from the different war taxes, such as sales tax, stamp tax and transportation tax, some of which he proposes to reduce. How is the House to know just what our revenue is likely to be next year unless we have some details? A statement of revenue showing an increase in our receipts of $11,900,000 is certainly an indication of improved conditions generally. The customs revenue shows an increase of $14,000,000. We do not know how much of this is due to increased valuation of goods for duty purposes and how much to a larger importation of dutiable goods.
I am certainly pleased that there is a reduction in our net debt and that in four years we have had a net reduction of $95,000,000. I am advised by the Department of Finance that our net debt to the end of the present fiscal year is estimated at $2,358,364,000. At the average rate of reduction which we have had for four years we may be able in the next one hundred years to retire our national debt, but it is hardly to be expected that that will be done if the present proposals are put into effect. It is the duty of the minister to consider and to present to parliament some definite plan for the systematic retirement of our national debt.
In comparing our revenue and expenditure, we should note that expenditure attributable to war is $162,922,000, or 45 per cent of our total expenditure. Revenue from war taxes amounts to $154,000,000. or $8,000,000 less than the expenditure attributable to war, or only 39.17 per cent of our revenue. The only changes which the minister proposes in this budget are reductions in war taxes, and these reductions are estimated at $27 000,000. The reductions in expenditure attributable to war are estimated at not more than $2,000,000, thus leaving our war charges at $160,000,000 with estimated revenue from war taxes of only $127,000,000, or 32 per cent of our estimated total revenue. I believe our war tax revenue should be sufficient to take care of expenditure attributable to war, but in this coming year apparently they will fall short by $33,000,000. If our former sources of revenue, namely customs duties and excise taxes, are sufficient to take care of ordinary and capital expenditures, and to reduce the national debt by $25,000,000, that is all that should be expected from them, and a reduction of five per cent in our customs tariff would afford more relief to business than the reduction which is proposed in the income tax.
The Budget-Mr. Coote

So far as the minister's proposals for reduction of taxation are concerned, I congratulate him upon his action in removing the tax from notes and overdrafts particularly. I believe his cut in the sales tax is a good move, and that it will help business generally, but I do not know yet whether we can afford to make the reduction.
As to the income tax reduction, I cannot agree with the minister that the income tax should be reduced at all. I think the reduction which was made in our income tax last year was quite sufficient, and I would urge that the income tax be maintained at least at its present level. The proposal of a reduction of ten per cent appears to me to be the first move in the elimination of this tax. I remarked a moment ago that it would take, at the present rate, one hundred years to pay off our war debt, but at the present rate of reduction in the income tax, it will take only ten years for that tax to disappear. Personally I would like to see the income tax maintained until all the war debt is paid. [DOT]
Just a few words in regard to the redemption of our debt. The minister shows a surplus on operations for the present fiscal year of $34,269,260. In another part of his address he states that the cash on hand from the previous year was $27,068,121, or a total of $61,337,381. Out of this amount he redeemed bonds in the present fiscal year amounting to $43,000,000, so it would appear that we will have on hand in cash at the end of this year $18,337,381. This is my own calculation; it is not mentioned in the minister's statement, Now there are maturing this year notes totalling $8,000,000, bonds due on November 1, 1927, amounting to $29,068,400, and bonds due on December 1, 1927, amounting to $63,437,250, or a total indebtedness maturing this year of $100,505,650. As I said before, we should have a cash surplus from the year 1926-1927 of $18,337,381 to apply on this amount, leaving the amount of $82,168,269 which may have to be refunded this year.
The proposal of the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) for refunding loans during the coming year at 4 per cent per annum is at least a very interesting one, and I think it should receive the careful consideration of the Minister of Finance and of the government. The speech of the hon. member for West Calgary was a very welcome change from the budget speeches which we have been in the habit of hearing from the front benches of the opposition during the last five years. His speech contained at least a new idea. My own suggestion for lowering the interest 
rate on the loans maturing this year would be to open a government savings bank at every money order post office in Canada, and to advertise that we will receive deposits bearing, if necessary, 3i per cent interest, and that these deposits will have the full guarantee of the Dominion behind them. I am sure that if that were done the minister would have no difficulty in securing enough deposits at 3J per cent to retire the bonds which mature this year.

Not at the present moment. I have been busy enough trying to get up a budget speech of my own, without going very deeply into the proposal of my hon. friend for West Calgary.
The minister gives us no definite statement of the revenue he anticipates for the year 1927-28, except to say that the tax reductions will reduce the revenue as compared with this year by S27,000,000. The revenue for 1926-27 is estimated at $394,870,000. If that is decreased next year by the $27,000,000 which the minister suggests, that will leave his revenue for 1927-28 at $367,870,000. There is no estimate of expenditure, except the opinion that it will be slightly larger than that of the present year. The main estimates as tabled are larger by the amount of $6,634,087. The expenditure for 1926-27 is estimated at $360,600,740, I think we are warranted in saying that the estimated expenditure for 1927-28 would be $6,634,087 more, which would make the amount $367,234,827, as compared with an estimated revenue of $367,780,000. That is, there would be an apparent surplus estimated for the coming year of approximately $500,000. I would like to ask the House where is there here any provision for the reduction of the debt next year? There is nothing contained in the minister's speech which would lead us to believe that there can be any reduction in the debt for the coming year if these budget proposals are carried out. There is only the pious wish that business conditions will be better next year, and therefore, that there will be a little more revenue with which to reduce the debt. I do not think any business house in Canada budgets in that manner, and I think this House and

The Budget-Mr. Coote
the government should budget so as to be prepared to reduce the national debt by some amount next year.
So far as western Canada is concerned, there is no indication that the coming year will be any better than the one we have just passed through. As a matter of fact our wheat is not grading as high, and we are not receiving as good a price. There is no indication there of any change for the better, and if for any reason we should have a poor crop the chances are that business conditions will not be so good and the revenue may not be quite as large as is now anticipated.
There is current talk in the newspapers and around the House of Commons that the government will this year have to provide some amount for increasing the subsidies to the maritime provinces. They may have to provide an amount to subsidize freight rates to the maritime provinces. I cannot see in this budget any provision for taking care of any such expenditure. I think it is only fair to say that if assistance in this manner is given to the maritime provinces there is bound to be a demand from the other provinces for increased subsidies, from provinces perhaps that can show just as good reasons why their subsidies should be increased. May I point out. to the House that the subsidies which the provinces are now receiving have a purchasing power of only a little over sixty cents on the dollar as compared with the time when they were granted, and I think there is no doubt in the world that the House will have to consider the question of whether the provincial subsidies generally will not have to be increased.
We have been discussing here for two days a bill to grant old age pensions in this country. If the government are sincere in their expressed belief that the provinces will pass the necessary legislation and come in under this old age pension scheme, we shall have to find some money to pay for our share of the old age pensions. I cannot see that there is any provision made in the budget for these old age pensions. I think that matter should be taken care of. It is quite possible the minister may have to pay some amount under the old age pension scheme in the coming fiscal year, because we are told that the British Columbia government at the present time is putting an old age pension bill through their legislature.
In view of all these circumstances, I doubt very much whether we are justified in giving effect to all the proposals for tax reduction which the minister has made, and it seems to
me there is no doubt in the world that the minister is making a mistake in proposing a reduction in the income tax, at any rate. The bonds which were issued for our war debt, which are such a millstone round this country's neck financially at the present time, are chiefly held by the class of people who pay a large share of this income tax. If this income tax is done away with you are going to entirely relieve this wealth from taxation.
The hon. member for West Calgary, seems to be in favour of replacing the income tax with a turnover tax, which I assume would be a direct tax on every business transaction. Surely a turnover tax must retard business more than the present income tax. We are told that the income tax retards the inflow of foreign capital. I cannot find anything in our history to confirm this view. Mr. Fiske of New York, a prominent authority on financial matters, estimates that the investment of American capital in Canada increased from $750,000,000 before the war to about $3,000,000,000 at the present time, and our income tax has been in force practically all that time.
In 1924 the Department of Commerce of the United States issued an estimate of British and American capital invested in Canada which showed a total of $1,890,000,000 British, $2,425,000,000 United States and $348,000,000 for other countries; or a total of $4,403,000,000 as of December 31st, 1923. Our own Bureau of Statistics issued a'statement last year showing a known new investment of American capital in Canadian securities amounting to $483,000,000 in the past four years.
In the face of these figures, I do not see how it can be contended that the income tax retards the investment of foreign capital in Canada. As a matter of fact what our industries need is not an increase of capital but an increased market for their products. In most manufacturing lines we are well supplied with factories, and in very few lines are our factories working to anything like full capacity. A reduction in income tax will not increase consumption, although it might release a very small amount for investment.
One of the difficulties of Canadian industry to-day is over-capitalization, and the capital is badly water-logged. I have before me a copy of a speech delivered by Colonel Arthur Hatch at the annual general meeting and dinner of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, held at the Windsor hotel, Montreal, June 1924, and at this dinner Colonel Hatch, discussing the development of Canadian industry during the fifty y7ear period from 1870
The Budget-Mr. Coote

to 1921, gave the following figures of the amount of capital invested, the employees' wages and the products:
Capital invested increased from $80,000,000 to $3,200,000,000.
Employees engaged increased from 188,000 to 517,000.
Salaries and wages increased from $40,000,000 to $581,000,000.
The value of their products increased from $222,000,000 to $2,748,000,000.
In other words-and this is Colonel Hatch's own statement-in the interval between 1870 and 1921 capital invested multiplied forty times; employees engaged three times; wages and salaries paid fourteen times and value of products, twelve times. I think there is evidence in that statement of the president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association that Canadian industries are very heavily overcapitalized. Any hon. member who was in this House tw'o years ago when we discussed the resolution moved by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) in connection with watered stock in Canadian companies does not need to be told of the vast amount of water there is in the stock of some of our manufacturing industries.
One advantage of the income tax is that it is inexpensive to collect. Last year we received from this source $55,571,000. at a collection cost of $1,724,000. We collected through the customs tariff last year $171,375000, which cost us to collect approximately $7,000,000. It is generally estimated that for every dollar the government collects in customs revenue from two to three times the amount is taken from the pockets of the people. A protective tariff is a tax on consumers, not for government purposes, but for private purposes, although incidentally it does bring in some revenue to the government. The best feature of the income tax, and one that I would like to commend to the attention of the House is that it is taken only from those who are able to pay. If it is replaced by a tax on commodities which people must purchase it' will have the effect of wholly releasing from taxation large amounts of capital which have been accumulated in the hands of a small number of men who are in control of our manufacturing industries and our financial institutions, and men who have accumulated fortunes out of the exploitation of our natural resources. Surely it would be unfair to allow the incomes from those large amounts which have been accumulated in the hands of a comparatively small number.of men, and in many cases through favours handed them by the

government, to escape taxation. The service rendered by the state to the citizen is largely the protection of his property. We even protect his property after he is dead, and see that it is handed over to the heirs whom he names. If this is so, why should not the citizen who has a larger share of wealth or income contribute according to the share which he has? Trade is restricted by taxation; this is especially true of customs, sales and turnover tax, all of which are a direct tax on commodities. The hon. member for West Calgary complained that the cost of living was too high, but if we are to replace the income tax with a turnover tax I do not think there is any doubt that the cost of living will be still higher. The income tax retards trade the least of any tax which we are imposing to-day. I do not think that statement can be challenged. The turnover tax, the sales tax and all consumption taxes, compel married men to pay more taxes than bachelors. They compel the man who has a family and children to pay more taxes than the couple who simply raise a poodle dog or a persian cat. If taxes are collected on consumption one man may have to contribute ten per cent of his income, while another may contribute only a fraction of one per cent, without any regard whatever to their ability to pay. I think that under an ideal system of government each citizen should contribute to the state an equal share of his time. Today each contributes his money, not time. If one man has an earning power much greater than another, why should he object to paying to the state a little more in the way of taxation?
The hon. member for West Calgary referred to certain principles of taxation laid down by Adam Smith. I have taken the trouble to again read certain portions of the Wealth of Nations and I should like to quote three or four of the requirements which Adam Smith thought should be met in levying taxation. This is the first requirement:
The subjects of every state ought to contribute towards the support of the government, as nearly as possible, in proportion to their respective abilities; that is, in proportion to the revenue which they respectively enjoy under the protection of the state.
Surely income tax meets that requirement. Then he says:
Every tax ought to be levied at the time, or in the manner, in which it is most likely to be convenient for the contributor to pay it.
The income tax meets that requirement, because the taxpayer does not have to pay the tax until he has earned it, and he does not

The Budget-Mr. Coote
have to pay it unless he has earned it. Adam Smith's next requirement is that:
Every tax ought to be so contrived as both to take out and to keep out of the pockets of the people as little as possible, over and above what it brings into the public treasury of the state.
I think the income tax meets that requirement; it is as inexpensive to collect as any tax we have. His final requirement is:
The tax which each individual is bound to pay ought to be certain as to the time of payment, the manner of payment, the quantity to be paid, ought all to be clear and plain to the contributor and to every other person.
I think the income tax also meets that requirement. If it does not, it is simply because the income tax law itself is not properly worded or properly administered. But I was so interested in reading the Wealth of Nations that I perused over twenty pages and came to this statement, which I believe may have a little bearing even to-day:
In the disorderly state of Europe during the prevalence of the feudal government, the sovereign *was obliged to content himself with taxing those who were too weak to refuse to pay taxes.
When I read that passage I naturally wondered whether in this present ease the government were following the line of least resistance and because there is much objection from these wealthy and powerful individuals and corporations they decided to reduce the income tax.
But Adam Smith is dead. I want to quote very briefly from a living political economist -Professor Stephen Leacock, of Montreal. Coming from such an authority as Professor Leacock, I think this should command the attention of the House.

But may I point-out to them that the Canadian manufacturers are the largest importers of United States goods? The list which the minister dealt with in his speech aggregates $224,000,000 out of total imports valued at $513,000,000. If you add to that list coal and other commodities which these manufacturers imported last year, I am sure you will see that they imported over half of the goods which appear as imports from the United States. The customs tariff allows our manufacturers to buy in a free market and to sell in a protected market; while the rest of the people, the farmers particularly, buy in a protected market and sell in a free trade market.
The collection of income tax is only a small attempt to remove some of the inequalities in the wealth of our citizens-inequalities caused, at least in part, by the operations of the tariff. The minister said that his aim has been to lighten the burden of taxation generally, that is on every taxpayer, rather than afford relief to special groups. But by reducing the in-

It is reduction in taxation affecting only about 10 per cent of our people-and the most highly favoured class at that. As the minister said last week, in reply to a speech from the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church):
The war is over, but it is not yet paid for.
The income tax should remain until it is paid for. With the exemptions from income tax now allowed, I cannot see that any hardship whatever is caused by this tax. The tax which to-day restricts trade more than any other form of taxation is the customs tariff. The situation in Europe became so acute that in October last a manifesto was published in London, signed by hundreds of the most prominent business men and bankers in Europe, as well as a large number of prominent bankers in the United States. It is worth noting that the manifesto was signed by the leading men in the countries which took part on either side in the Great war, it was signed bv men in

The Budget-Mr. Coote
England, France, Italy and Belgium as well as by men in Germany, Austria and Hungary. It is one of the most important documents given to the business world for a long time, and is well worth incorporating in Hansard. It is too long to read here, but if I have the permission of the House it may appear in Hansard without being read, as it will only take about a page. It should be remembered also that this statement is not made by Adam Smith or by any other man who lived a hundred years ago, when conditions were very different; it was written by men living today, some of the most astute business men in the world, speaking from their own personal' experience and observation. The statement is as follows.
The manifesto printed below, called A Plea for the Removal of Restrictions upon European Trade, was published in London on October 19.
We desire, as business men, to draw attention to certain grave and disquieting conditions which, in our judgment, are retarding the return to prosperity.
It is difficult to view without dismay the extent to which tariff barriers, special licenses, and prohibitions since the war have been allowed to interfere with international trade and to prevent it from flowing in its natural channels. At no period in recent history has freedom from such restrictions been more needed to enable traders to adapt themselves to new and difficult conditions. And at no period have impediments to trading been more perilously multiplied without a true appreciation of the economic consequences involved.
The break-up of great political units in Europe dealt a heavy blow to international trade. Across large areas in which the inhabitants had been allowed to exchange their products freely, a number of new frontiers were erected and jealously guarded by customs barriers. Old markets disappeared. Racial animosities were permitted to divide communities whose interests were inseparably connected. The situation is not unlike that which would be created if a confederation of states were to dissolve the ties which bind them, and to proceed to penalize and hamper, instead of encouraging, each other's trade. Few will doubt that under such conditions the prosperity of such a country would rapidly decline.
To mark and defend these new frontiers in Europe, licences, tariffs, and prohibitions were imposed, with results which experience shows already to have been unfortunate for all concerned. One state lost its supplies of cheap food, another its supplies of cheap manufactures. Industries suffered for want of coal, factories for want of raw materials. Behind the customs barriers new local industries were started, with no real economic foundation, which could only be kept alive in the face of competition by raising the barriers higher still. Railway rates, dictated by political considerations, have made transit and freights difficult and costly. Prices have risen, artificial dearness has been created. Production as a whole has been diminished. Credit has contracted and currencies have depreciated. Too many states, in pursuit of false ideals of national interest, have imperiled their own welfare and
22649-32J
lost sight of the common interests of the world, by basing their commercial relations on the economic folly which treats all trading as a form of war.
There can be no recovery in Europe till politicians in all territories, old and new, realize that trade is not war but a process of exchange, that in time of peace our neighbours are our customers, and that their prosperity is a condition of our own well-being. If we check their dealings, their power to pay their debts diminishes and their power to purchase our goods is reduced. Restricted imports involve restricted exports, and no nation can afford to lose its export trade. Dependent as we all are upon imports and exports, and upon the processes of international exchange, we cannot view without grave concern a policy which means the impoverishment of Europe.
Happily there are signs that opinion in all countries is awaking at last to the dangers ahead. The League of Nations and the International Chamber of Commerce have been labouring to reduce to a minimum all formalities, prohibitions, and restrictions, to remove inequalities of treatment in other matters than tariffs, to facilitate the transport of passengers and goods. In some countries powerful voices are pleading for the suspension of tariffs altogether. Others have suggested the conclusion for long periods of commercial agreements embodying in every case the most favoured-nation clause. Some states have recognized in recent treaties the necessity of freeing trade from the restrictions which depress it. And experience is slowly teaching others that the breaking-down .of the economic barriers between them may prove the surest remedy for the stagnation which exists. On the valuable political results which might flow from such a Policy, from the substitution of good-will for ill-will, of co-operation for exclusiveness we will not dwell. But we wish to place on record our conviction that the establishment of economic freedom is the best hope of restoring the commerce and the credit of the world.
A reduction in the taxation on consumption helps to increase business and encourages the producer to increase his volume, which can scarcely be said of a reduction in income tax. A reduction in the customs tariff or in the sales tax would undoubtedly have the effect of increasing business. Last year the minister reduced the tariff on automobiles, and we were warned by the Conservatives that the automobile industry would be ruined. The condition of the industry to-day proves that it has been greatly benefited by those reductions. I have here an advertisement which I took from the Calgary Albertan last August; it was inserted by Dodge Brothers of Canada Limited, and states that for the three weeks ending July 17, 89 per cent more cars and trucks were delivered to customers than during the same period in the previous year. Mr. Speaker, it has been customary in Canada for many years for parties in this House to outline to 'the country their policy on
economic matters at the time the budget is before the House. It is a rare thing, so far as I know, for budgets to be brought down without an amendment being presented by some party.
I may say that our group have given very careful consideration to this budget. There are some things in it that we approve of; there are some things that we disapprove of. There are proposals contained in the budget that should not be there, and things which it ought to contain are not there. Under the circumstances we have to decide whether the
The Budget-Mr. Coote

omissions are important enough to warrant the moving of an amendment to the budget. So far as the present budget is concerned, we have come to the conclusion that the principle of direct taxation, consciously or unconsciously, is being attacked in favour of indirect taxation. We believe this is a backward step in our taxation policy, and that the question is of such importance that the members of the House should have the opportunity of placing themselves on record in regard to this principle.
We believe the Finance minister has no good excuse for refusing to suggest some reductions in the tariff simply because the tariff board has a number of applications before it on which it has not reported. We cannot allow the board to become an excuse for inaction or indifference on the part of the government, and the seeming indisposition to carry out that policy as expressed in their platform, and in the utterances of their leader and the members of their party generally.
We are also impressed with the fact that no attempt is being made by the Minister of Finance to deal in a systematic way with the reduction of the national debt, the interest on which at the present time is absorbing 36 per cent of our total revenue. Under the circumstances we feel that it is our duty to present an amendment to this House. I therefore move:
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted
therefor:
Whilst recognizing the advisability of certain minor changes proposed, this House regrets that the budget as presented by the honourable Minister of Finance contains no effective provision for the reduction in the high cost of living, in so far as such is due to the protective tariff;
That the budget shows a further departure from the principle of direct and visible taxation based on the ability to pay.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is
with a feeling of considerable satisfaction that I rise on this occasion to pay tribute to my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on the favourable statement of the country's affairs which he has presented this year in his budget speech. Not only has the Minister of Finance reason to feel proud but the country as well should feel highly pleased at the statement which he presented to the House.

The budget as delivered deals with the relief of taxation, and I wish to compliment the Minister of Finance on having been able to deal so directly, in the second consecutive year, with the burden of taxation which falls on the average citizen. I think the Minister of Finance should feel very gratified to-day at the manner in which his budget pronouncements have been received. He has been the recipient of compliments, not only from the press, but from citizens throughout the Dominion of Canada; and I am quite sure that no one in this Dominion will hereafter make so bold as to prophesy the ruin of Canadian industry by reason of the action of this government.
I wish also to pay a compliment to the ex-Minister of Finance, the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett). While we might expect from an hon. member with the political knowledge and the legal and financial experience of my hon. friend a speech worthy of any subject, it was to me a great satisfaction that from the opposition side of the House we had on that occasion a speech which was not purely destructive but which contained many constructive suggestions, and I wish to compliment my hon. friend thereon.
The statement presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) was a plain, uncoloured statement of facts; a statement which could easily be understood and the accuracy of which could not be questioned. And this is as it should be for the presentation of our annual statement should at all times be so clear as to leave no question as to its accuracy. I feel sure that in this instance the Minister of Finance has met tha't requisite. I also wish to compliment the minister on presenting a statement in which he does not take to himself all the credit for conditions as they exist throughout the country. He rather leaves it to the good judgment of the House to decide whether or not his policies have been beneficial to the national life.
His budget deals particularly with relief from taxation, and he chooses on this occasion as in the last budget to make that relief apply more especially to direct taxation. The statement of the affairs of this country which the budget revealed surely is one which will enable us as a people to go forward with courage and confidence into the future, filled with the realization that we are now indeed on the verge of an era of prosperity. I believe the budget itself will accentuate that condition of affairs.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) has criticised at considerable length the in-

The Budget-Mr. Malcolm
come tax reductions proposed by the Minister of Finance, and I wish to refer briefly to his criticism. The hon. gentleman endeavours to create the impression that the whole load of the income tax is on that section of the Canadian people possessed of higher incomes, and that it is therefore a good form of taxation to keep at a maximum. It will be remembered that the Minister of Finance in his budget last year increased the income tax exemptions and the benefits that were derived from last year's budget were practically altogether in favour of those with lower incomes. I believe it will foe found that as a result of last year's income tax reductions about 75,000 of our citizens were relieved from income taxation altogether. There were only about 150,000 who came under the old act. Is it not fair that when so many have been entirely relieved, the budget presented this year by the minister should take some cognizance of that fact and make a reduction such as has been made all along the line? I consider that the reduction in income tax made by the minister this year is an extremely fair one. As a matter of fact it is simply this: when the income tax is computed by the established method, a straight discount of 10 per cent is given on the income tax so computed. That is equality in relief from taxation.
My hon. friend worries as to the revenues of the country and our ability to pay off the national debt. In 1921-22 we collected about
S78,000,000 from income tax. In the yeara following the amounts were in the neighbourhood of $55,000,000 to $00,000,000 per annum or less. Last year it was estimated by the minister that the loss due to his reductions in income tax would amount to about $14,000,000, but it has turned out that the loss of income tax due to those reductions will be only about $8,000,000. This is attribuable to several reasons. The general increase in prosperity in the country has undoubtedly been a factor in giving better returns on invested capital. The larger agricultural wealth, referred to by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) undoubtedly played an important part in the creation of the increased wealth of the community. Furthermore from time to time tax-free securities have been called in. It is reasonable therefore to suppose that with continued prosperity there will not be as serious a falling off in the income tax collections as some people believe.
The hon. member for Macleod stated that our income tax does not prevent United States capital from coming to Canada, and I would like if I might be permitted, to clarify
his mind in respect to that matter. To a certain extent it is true, in that United States capital which comes to Canada is held by citizens of the United States who own such securities on which income tax is not payable* in Canada. That is the justification for the corporation tax. The corporation tax of 9 per cent is the one method the Minister of Finance has to get at the large United States company operating in 'Canada, the dividends of which company go t,o the shareholders or stockholders residing in the United States. So long, however, as Canada retains a high ratio of income tax on large investments just so long will we not be able to get investors of large amounts of capital to become Canadian citizens and pay income tax in this country. That is the point in question. Is it not natural to expect that the converse will also happen, namely, that men possessed of decided wealth in Canada, who do not care much whether they make their permanent home, in let us say, the city of Montreal, or their winter home in the south, should (finally establish their residences in the United States and pay their income tax there under less severe rates? If the hon. member for Macleod reviews the situation, I believe he will come to that conclusion.
I consider that he is also wrong in stating that the income tax reduction is not a popular move with the agriculturist. I do not think anyone can question the interest taken in agriculture by the Premier of Manitoba. Premier Bracken is probably as much interested as any man in western Canada in the agriculturists, and I would inform my hon. friend that last week Premier Bracken brought down a budget announcing a reduction in the income tax.
I now wish to refer briefly to the reduction made by the minister in 'the stamp tax on commercial documents. There is a very-erroneous impression abroad as to who pays this tax. To me it is burdensome and paid by the wrong class of people altogether. It cannot be denied that in every instance it is the debtor who pays the tax. A debtor has obligations enough in paying his debt in addition to the ordinary banking charges on commercial paper, without having ten or twelve dollars added to his note in the form of taxes, and without the necessity every time his note is renewed at the bank, or a cheque given, of covering the whole back of it with stamps. In reducing this tax the minister is appreciably relieving those in our country who are heavy borrowers and who are paying

The Bxcdget-Mr. Malcolm
their bills. The banks do not pay this tax. The commercial houses do not pay it. In every instance the man who meets the obligation is charged with the cost of the stamps which have to go on his paper. There is every justice in making the tax on commercial paper as reasonable an amount as can be set. I am glad the tax is being continued from the standpoint of revenue, but I am glad it is being removed in its present excessive form.
With regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Macleod concerning the sales tax, I wish to make just this observation, that I have never been an enthusiastic supporter of the sales tax. I think it drives up the cost of merchandise, it is unquestionably pyramided, and it eventually slows up merchandising and trading. On the other hand, no better illustration can be given of the difficulty of removing a tax once it has been established than the problem of the sales tax. Many people have argued in favour of the complete and speedy removal of this form of taxation. Many representations have been made to the minister and much has been said in the press in favour of this. But the minister must take into consideration the very disturbing effect the sudden removal of a full five per cent of the value of the merchandise would have on business. Merchants and wholesalers all over the country have enormous stocks of merchandise, of a value probably many times the total capital invested in their businesses and if the government were to make a sudden reduction of five per cent in the value of the stocks held, it might mean a fifty per cent reduction in the total assets of those businesses. Therefore, I compliment the minister in doing what he has done, in making a gradual reduction in the sales tax, and my advice to him would be to continue with this gradual reduction, such as can be absorbed without causing any very great hardship to the merchants, until the tax is finally eliminated.
My hon. friend from West Calgary, the ex-Minist.er of Finance (Mr. Bennett) made a statement in his speech on Thursday to which I wish to refer. While it is very easy for me to admire a speech made by my hon. friend, it is not always so easy to agree with the premises on which he bases his argument or with the conclusions at which he arrives. He made the general statement that the Dominion government took from the people of Canada in the year just closed $1.64 more per capita than it had taken in the previous year. First, I wish to correct my hon. friend as to a slight inaccuracy in his mathematical calculation.

He took the difference in the two years' revenue and divided that by the population of Canada in June, 1926. Now in June, 1925, we had a population in Canada of 9,268,000; in June, 1926, we had a population of 9,390,000.

speechtext: I might say to the minister that no allowance was made for the numbers of people who had left Canada between 1925 and 1926, and I took the figure as given by the department for June, 1926.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's remarks are quite in order. I took the same figures as were given to him for June, 1926, but I also got from the department the figure 9,268,000 as the population of Canada for June, 1925. Now if we divide the revenue for 1925 by that figure, we find that $35.34 was the total per capita amount of federal -taxation for the fiscal year 1925, whereas dividing the population of 9,390,000, the figure for June, 1926, into the revenue of $343,000,000 collected in that year, gives us a per capita contribution of $36.53, resulting in an increased per capita contribution, not of $1.64 as stated by my hon. friend, but of $1.19.
But aside from this slight inaccuracy, Mr. Speaker, we cannot accept the very simple method of my hon. friend in arriving at the per capita contribution of the people of Canada to the total of taxation. My hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) referred a moment ago to the very heavy increase in the importation of raw material by the manufacturers of this country. That is quite true, and that becomes a very important factor with respect to the duty collected when these goods are manufactured here and exported to another country. My hon. friend from Macleod assumes that all the goods imported by the Canadian manufacturers are free of duty. As a matter of fact, all equipment used by Canadian industrial plants which manufactured for export pays duty, and there is no rebate, and even where there is provision for rebate, in no case is the total duty rebated. I desire therefore to point out to the House that a considerable contribution to the exchequer results from duties paid on equipment and plant, and merchandise imported which is afterwards exported to other countries of the world. This particular source of revenue forms, I believe, an increasingly larger and more important part of the revenues of this country as the years go by.
There is also another matter which my hon. friend from Macleod has I fear entirely misunderstood. He speaks of the excise revenue as being a per capita revenue. Personally I

The Budget-Mr. Malcolm
do not think that excise revenue can be treated as a per capita revenue at all. I do not believe that all people contribute equally to the excise revenue. I do not think that my hon. friend from West Calgary, for instance, and a few other gentlemen are charged with as large a proportion of excise taxation as some other people.
There is another factor which is very important in the distribution of revenue per capita, and it is this. In times of prosperity, is it not true that the wealthier of our citizens purchase more luxuries, which in Canada are dutiable, and thereby contribute in greater proportion to the revenues of the country? And is it not still more true, Mr. Speaker, that when times are prosperous, the average citizen indulges in the purchase of more articles, more comforts for his home, thus by the purchase of two articles instead of one, adding to the total revenue of the country?
But then, after all, supposing we did collect more revenue last year than the year previous. Did any harm result? I submit not. My hon. friend from West Calgary himself pointed out that as a result of that increased revenue and the lessening of expenditure we were able to do what my hon. friend from Macleod says we are not doing fast enough-pay $13,000,000 off our deadweight debt. Surely there is ground for satisfaction in that.
My hon. friend analyses under the heads of the various departments the money extracted from the people by means of taxation. In this connection I think he will agree with me, that the $1.50 per capita deficit of our Post Office department is not one which can be very much questioned. We as a people in Canada have chosen to accept a uniform postage rate from the Atlantic to the Pacific, rather than a rate based on mileage, the same as transportation. Canada has been built up by those who have pioneered the vast spaces, and it is only logical that those of us who live in the more densely settled districts, where the distribution of mail matter is much more economic, should be more heavily charged than those who live in the sparsely settled districts. The whole question of postal revenue is one of national policy, and I believe that every man in the country to-day is in favour of a uniform postage rate and a uniform parcels post rate; I believe that every man in the country is in favour of rural mail delivery in order to make the lives of the people in the country a little more pleasant. I have never found any difference in policy as between any two governments in Canada on this question, and
I believe that if there is a slight deficit in the returns of the Post Office department this year, the Canadian people are quite satisfied that those who live in the more heavily settled districts, and receive the cheapest service so far as actual cost is concerned, should pay a greater proportion of the cost of the whole service.
I wish to refer for a moment to the criticism of the hon. member for Macleod as regards the budget and the tariff. The budget has announced no tariff changes this year, and I presume that that furnishes legitimate ground for criticism by those who want tariff changes either up or down. Many applications for advances and many applications for decreases in the tariff have been laid before the tariff board. There were charges both ways. It , was charged that the high tariff made living expensive. It was also charged that the lowness of the tariff made it difficult to conduct industry in this country, and that unemployment was caused thereby. Much data has been collected by the board, but, Mr. Speaker, not nearly all the data that is necessary to substantiate the claims of those who are seeking an increase in the tariff has yet been collected, more particularly with respect to the major industries, steel, woollens, and boots and shoes. Nor has there been anything like unanimity in their arguments on the part of those asking for tariff increases. People in various branches of the steel industry, for instance, in their presentations before the board have held diametrically opposed views as to whether the tariff should be increased on certain articles, articles, for instance, which are the finished product of one mill and the raw material of another. Therefore, until *these diametrically opposed views can be reconciled it is only reasonable to suppose that in this major industry the minister could not deal with the request for advances in the tariff. The case of the tariff on woollen goods has yet to be heard and when it comes up the same condition may arise. Various branches of the industry will probably hold different views. There may have to be revision of classifications, and a considerable time must elapse before the board can collect the required data. With regard to the question of boots and shoes, hearings have taken place but I understand further hearings are to be held. Truthfully it can be said that in no industry of major importance has all the evidence been brought down or all the facts established for submission to the government.

Is it not true that something over forty odd reports have been made to the minister?

speechtext: Only twelve? It must have been more than that.

maintopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS-INTERNAL TRADE BRANCH
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman heard my statement. I will eome to that question in a moment. The hon. member for West Calgary in a speech some time ago stated that the difficulty experienced in arriving at a satisfactory conclusion as to what measure of tariff should be applied was very great. To quote his actual words, in the House of Commons debate, May 18, 1926, he said:
We realize, as every man in this House must realise, how difficult it is to understand fully the complex operations of the tariff, and come to an adequate and proper conclusion with respect to how far-reaching its ramifications may be.
Just so. With regard to the major industries they are so complex that a great deal of evidence, has to be compiled after the first representations are made, and on these major industries, regarding which the country is looking for decisions, there has not yet been sufficient evidence compiled to justify the minister in making a decision. Furthermore, it has been pointed out by my hon. friend that the tariff board is not making definite findings, that it is only an information-collecting bureau. When this information has been collected and placed before the Minister of Finance, the government itself must assume responsibility for the action taken as a result of the findings. It is therefore logical to assume that some consideration must yet be given even to those cases to which my hon. friend referred a moment ago in his question. I wish to point out to the hon. member that the items which have been before the board, and on which the board has secured information and submitted it to the government, number ten or twelve- I think, thirteen altogether. Now there is no item of such major importance as to justify a revision of the tariff this year. They are small items indeed. An application was made for a reduction of the duty on calcium chloride A reduction was asked for on certain pumps! An increase was asked on piano player rolls, though the matter is really a question of classification in the Customs department, as to whether they are to be classed as sheet music or musical instruments. A reduction was asked in the tariff on imported candles. An application was made with regard to gabardine cloth, and I suppose the minister saw no particular reason why he should consider that application before he had reviewed the whole textile industry. And so on all down the line. All

the matters that have been reported upon by the board are comparatively of so little economic importance to the country that I think the minister has done wisely in withholding his decision on that group, until he could deal with the major industries. I will however say this-that when the evidence and the facts are brought down they will be reviewed, and on the evidence submitted and having regard to the economic conditions in this country, the government will bring down its policy for reduction or increase, and will be prepared, as it has always been, to stand by its decision.
If some of my friends who are strongly in favour of no increase in the customs tariff were very wise they would also be very patient. Patience is the course of wisdom, if you are looking for no increase, for the reason that the industries which two years ago were in a stagnant 'condition are this year prosperous, and it will be more difficult, as prosperity continues, to establish a case for increase in tariff. I believe that this year we have got into our stride and that manufacturers are in a better position than heretofore. As a result of that many industries which were blaming the tariff for their troubles will be no longer inclined to do so, because the trouble has disappeared. In last year's budget the most important item of change was the reduction of the duty on motor cars, and the establishment of a qualifying content of fifty per cent Canadian labour and material. I do not wish to embarrass any hon. members opposite by quoting to them their speeches regarding the dire disaster that would befall the automobile industry, because I feel that genuine alarm was felt by them, as well as by some on this side of the House. The fact however remains that the important item with respect to the motor car tariff reductions was the fifty per cent qualifying content made necessaiy. To-day everyone is agreed as to the wisdom of the policy which the minister announced in last year's budget, that before certain rebates of duties would be granted to American concerns manufacturing in Canada Canadian labour and material must be used to the extent of fifty per cent. We realize the great wealth and resources of the American republic, and we are willing to admit that probably our geographical position deprives us of many of the commodities which we would desire in this country-many commodities which are necessary to the economic life of the country. The hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Gott) I think had a question on the order paper to-day in regard to agricultural imports into Canada. Such agricultural imports consist largely of tropical

The Budget-Mr. Malcolm
fruits and vegetables which we do not grow, and which though termed agricultural products, are entirely different from those produced in this country. We need these commodities, but our climatic conditions do not permit us to produce them. We do not for example produce cotton and rubber. Our limited production of certain commodities and the limited production in other parts of the empire of commodities such as we produce, has induced the government to support a policy of British preferential tariffs. There is no question but that the policy of a British preferential tariff, not as we extend it to some other countries, but as some other countries extend it to us in return, has induced many manufacturers to come to Canada to establish branch plants. If an industry comes to Canada and is merely an assembling plant it is not of very much consequence to Canada, and the best way to turn that assembling plant into a real manufacturing plant that will give employment to Canadian labour and build up the industrial growth of the country is to stipulate that before the plant will be given a preference in this country the production must be a certain specified percentage Canadian.
Premier Bruce and Premier Coates visited Canada on their way home from the Imperial conference, and we were glad to have them honour us with their company. They both asked us in effect: " Is it reasonable that we should give to you a preference on motor cars, of which we buy practically our whole supply from you, unless those cars are Canadian-made and not merely assembled?" No one can gainsay the wisdom of the Australian and New Zealand governments in inserting a clause in their custom tariffs for that purpose. What our Minister of Finance did by his last year's budget was to compel our automobile manufacturers to bring their cars up to the 50 per cent point of Canadian content. Had he not done so then, the motor car manufacturers would have found themselves forced to take that course by virtue of the customs regulations of the countries to which they export their cars. With the permission of the House I should like to place on Hansard a table showing the production of passenger automobiles, trucks and chassis in the Dominion during the past eight years.

In 1919 W'e produced 87,000 motor cars in round figures. That production gradually increased until by 1923 it had reached 147,000. In 1924 there was a decrease. In 1925 both export and domestic business improved and the total production reached 162,000; while in the year just closed the production increased to 205,000, about half being for domestic consumption and half for export. There is no cause to worry about the employment of labour when we have such a big increase in production. I may say that there has been a very material improvement in employment conditions in our motor car factories. Not only that, but any man who is interested in the great number of supply houses-and there are several such men in this House-representing a variety of genuine Canadian industries, owned by Canadian capital, founded and developed by Canadians, is aware that those industries have benefited to a very great extent because the motor car manufacturers have had to place their orders for supplies with such Canadian industries, thereby giving employment all over the country.
There is a very great difference, Mr. Speaker, between an industry in Canada which was built up by Canadians and an industry established here for the definite purpose of securing the benefit of certain preferential tariffs. Especially is this difference realized when we consider that in the latter case most of the stock is owned in a foreign country, and the dividends do not pay income tax here except perhaps on a small percentage of the stock held by people domiciled in this country. The greatest benefit of the 50 per cent requirement laid down in last year's budget has been in the form of orders from our motor car manufacturers for other Canadian industries.
With regard to employment, Mr. Speaker, many statements have been made. The statistical branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce keeps a record of 6,000 industries, which make monthly returns to the department. This number remains constant, because only when one industry passes out is another taken in. From those returns an index number of employment is carefully compiled. The peak of the post war boom was in January, 1920, and accordingly the index number for that year was placed at 100. By 192!l the index number had fallen to 87.4 and from that time on there has been a gradual rise, until to-day the index number is at 98.4. In other words, there has been an increase in the index number of practically 11 points. Every point in the index number represents over 8,000 people. The total increase in employment, as estimated for me to-day by the bureau, shows a gain in all our industries of about 100,000 since 1921. This cannot be

The Budget-Mr. Malcolm
said to apply to the motor car industry alone; it is spread over every industry in the Dominion. A population of 100,000 workers unquestionably means a total population of about half a million, assuming that it is true to say that those dependent upon industrial workers represent a ratio of 5 to 1. I believe therefore that the industrial improvement in this country during the past four years represents an improvement in population of 500,000.
This increase in industrial development can best 'be judged by the rise of security values, and there is no one in this House at the moment but is willing to admit that we have had a tremendous increase in our security values. The common stocks of our banks have improved; that speaks well for the solidity of our financial houses and for the volume of transactions. Our power stocks have all improved; that speaks well for the consumption of power in this country-and we must remember that the greatest consumer of power is industry. Our manufacturing stocks have also improved, and not even in some of the lines of industry for which members of parliament are wont to beseech further consideration of customs tariff do we find any necessity for assistance.
The hon. leader of the opposition, I think, was trying to take a fall out of me in his speech on the address when he asked me to give to tariffs for other industries the same support I gave to a tariff for the furniture industry. May I point out that the furniture tariff is 30 per cent general, 27| per cent intermediate and 18 per cent British preferential as against a general tariff of 35 per cent on all woollens, an intermediate of 25 per cent on knitted goods, 27 per cent on flannels, 29f per cent on fabrics, socks and stockings, and1 a British preferential of 18 per cent on knitted goods and flannels, 22| per cent on socks and stockings and 24J per cent on fabrics. It is therefore evident that the furniture industry is not one of our highly protected industries, and I do not think our furniture or woodworking manufacturers-and they are not asking for increased protection -can show as rapid a rise in the value of their stock as can Penman's-from 152 to 186 in two years; as can the Dominion Textile common stock-68 to 107; as can Canada Cement-92l to 131 in a like period. I could give a long list of other industries whose stocks show a similarly rapid rise, but I will not weary the House with further examples. No, Mr. Speaker, the position of the industrial life of this country the government does not take entire credit for; but the government does take credit for making the pathway along which business can proceed profitably and

easily and to that extent it is entitled to credit.
The business of this country is expanding, as my hon. friend said, owing, for one thing, to the enormous production of our agricultural wealth. It is also expanding because there has been a very great improvement in our exports of manufactured products. As the hon. member for Macleod mentioned, our exports are 56 per cent agricultural. Let me ask him what the other 44 per cent represents. From year to year we have been developing a greater market abroad for our manufactured goods. Our trade commissioners, established by Sir George Foster when he was Minister of Trade and Commerce, have done good work in various parts of the worid. Canadian implements and Canadian automobiles are becoming well known in all parts of the Empire. Our industrial life is growing apace with our agricultural wealth, and I believe every hon. gentleman will agree with me that that ia what we desire. We do not want to be a onesided nation. As my hon. friend the former member for Lambton said, we want to be a well-rounded household, able as far as possible to create 'wealth within ourselves, but able to sell our wealth in the form of merchandise to other countries.
My hon. friend from West Calgary referred to the exhaustion of our mineral wealth In the course of his speech following the introduction of the budget he mentioned that we exported a tremendous amount of minerals. It is true that we exported about 852,000,000 worth to the United States but we also imported from the United States $83,000,000 worth of minerals in the same time. That is not a very bad state of affairs.

It is true that we exported a million dollars worth of nickel, but we imported a million and a half dollars worth of aluminum. We did not export any iron ore, but we imported a considerable amount, worth a million and a half dollars. It is true that we have exported gold, but I would like to ask my hon. friend of what use gold is if we do not export it. We cannot use it all in the fine arts. Gold is a medium of exchange; it is very valuable, but we in this country do not want to hoard all the gold we produce. We imported $50,000,000 worth of coal, but my hon. friend has a most logical mind, and I would suggest that since the exportation of mineral is an exhaustion of our mineral wealth, surely the importation of coal is a conservation.

The Budget-Mr. Malcolm

speechtext:
I must say that my friend even went further than the leader of the opposition, who in his speech on the address said it was all right to export farm products as they were replaceable. My hon. friend said the other day, however, that they were not replaceable, to a certain extent, as they exhausted the soil. He recalls to my mind a very frugal and cautious countryman of mine in the county of Bruce; he wasna' happy when he had no crop because he had no siller, and he wasna' happy when he had big crops because it was hard on the land.
Even in connection with immigration, which is so much discussed, the figures are improving. Last year 134,984 immigrants came to our shores as against 84,000 registered in 1925, but most significant of all, and the thing I think we should be most happy over, was the fact that 48,000 Canadians came back from the United States, and at the border declared their intention of residing in Canada. We are not increasing our population nearly as fast as we should, but I believe that if the feeling of optimism and of loyalty to our government and institutions is preserved; if those of us who are out of power quit knocking our country and all join together, our immigration figures will rapidly improve. It is little wonder that people went from Canada when half the people were saying Canada was not fit to live in. I am glad to compliment my friend the ex-Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett) for giving the lead to the note of optimism and for pointing out to this House that while there is something to be gained by destructive criticism, much more can be done by constructive suggestion.
The volume of business done in this country has been enormously increased in the past year; the figures of the clearing houses in the different banking centres show that in 1926 they handled commercial paper to the extent of $30,358,000,000. In 1925 the amount was $28,126,000,000, and in 1924 $27,-
157.000,000. Therefore it will be seen that the financial transactions in this country have
been gradually improving, and conditions becoming better. Both official and non-official figures on building construction show a marked improvement. MacLean's building reports show contracts awarded in the past year to the amount of $373,000,000, in round figures, while the Statistical Bureau, which deals with sixty-three cities, reports a figure of $156,000,000; in both cases the transactions show an increase of 25 per cent. My hon. friend referred to life insurance, which is another good indication, Life insurance in force is amazingly large in Canada; in 1921 the figure was $2,934,000,000, and at the end of 1925 that had reached $4,159,000,000. It is estimated by competent authorities that to-day the Canadian people are carrying insurance on thear lives to the extent of $4,500,000,000. Surely that is an indication of prosperity, and it has taken place in the short period of five years. Another good indication of wealth is the number of motor car registrations. Thar number has increased from 465,000 in 1921 to 728,000 in 1925, which is an indication of the ability of people to purchase luxuries. The number of telephones in use in Canada, also an indication of the ability of the people to procure conveniences rose from 902,000 in 1921 to 1,114,000 in 1925.
Perhaps the best indication of all as to our condition is the Canadian National Railways. In 1921 the government of my honoured leader came into power facing a deficit in operation of $11,000,000. The fact cannot be gainsaid that the rapid change in the financial condition of the National railways, which I will leave the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) to enlarge upon, has been a very great factor in reducing our taxation. In the five years the situation has so changed that to-day we have an operating surplus of over $46,000,000, making a total change of about $58,000,000 in that short time. I will deal in a moment with the expenditures and receipts of the country in this connection, but before doing that I would like to make one other reference. When a people numbering 9,000,000 are able to handle $30,000,000,000 worth of transactions through banking houses in a year, when they are able at the same time to pay premiums on $4,500,000,000 of life insurance; when they are able to pay taxes amounting to $35 per capita and, in addition, increase their savings in actual cash in the banks to the enormous total of $1,372.000,000, they are not in very bad condition.
